prompt: What does CSMA/CA contribute to ordinary Wi-Fi operation?
options: Listening, waiting and backoff to reduce contention collisions
Full-duplex transmission and reception on the same ordinary radio
A dedicated collision-free channel for each associated station
Guaranteed retransmission-free delivery once a client associates
explanation: CSMA/CA has stations listen before sending and back off when the channel is busy. This reduces collisions but does not remove them, retries or interference.

whyWrong.1: An ordinary Wi-Fi radio is half duplex.
whyWrong.2: Association does not give a station its own channel.
whyWrong.3: Association does not guarantee error-free delivery.

prompt: For neighboring APs on the North American 2.4 GHz 20 MHz plan, which two statements are correct? Choose two.
options: A 40 MHz channel creates more independent frequency choices
Adjacent channel numbers have centers only 5 MHz apart
Channels 1, 2 and 3 provide three separate occupied ranges
Channels 1, 6 and 11 are the usual nonoverlapping reuse set
A different SSID lets nearby APs ignore shared airtime
explanation: Adjacent 2.4 GHz channel centers are only 5 MHz apart, so a 20 MHz channel overlaps its neighbors. Channels 1, 6 and 11 are the nonoverlapping set.

whyWrong.0: A wider channel uses more spectrum and leaves fewer independent choices.
whyWrong.2: Channels 1, 2 and 3 overlap each other.
whyWrong.4: A different SSID does not change the frequency, so the APs still share airtime.

prompt: Why can an AP using a DFS-required 5 GHz channel leave that channel even when its clients have strong signals?
options: SSID uniqueness requires each AP to change its channel periodically
Radar protection requires it to vacate after a radar detection
A strong client signal causes a mandatory radio power shutdown
A WPA2 key renewal requires a different center frequency
explanation: DFS requires an AP to leave a channel when it detects radar, which protects the radar users of that spectrum. Client signal strength does not override this.

whyWrong.0: SSID uniqueness has nothing to do with DFS.
whyWrong.2: Signal strength does not trigger a DFS channel change.
whyWrong.3: Key renewal does not change the channel.

prompt: Wi-Fi 6E extends which radio technology into compatible 6 GHz equipment?
explanation: Wi-Fi 6E is 802.11ax extended into the 6 GHz band, and both AP and client need 6 GHz hardware.

whyWrong.1: 802.11n uses 2.4 and 5 GHz.
whyWrong.2: 802.11a is an older 5 GHz standard.
whyWrong.3: 802.11ac is a 5 GHz standard.

prompt: A WLAN is configured for WPA2 with a pre-shared key (WPA2-PSK). Which authentication and encryption pair does that describe?
options: One shared passphrase, with AES-CCMP encryption
Individual EAP credentials, with AES-CCMP encryption
SAE password authentication, with required PMF
One shared passphrase, with TKIP encryption
explanation: WPA2-PSK is WPA2-Personal: all clients share one passphrase and the traffic is encrypted with AES-CCMP.

whyWrong.1: Individual EAP credentials mean WPA2-Enterprise, not PSK.
whyWrong.2: SAE with required PMF is WPA3-Personal.
whyWrong.3: TKIP is the original WPA's encryption, not WPA2's.

prompt: Which two statements describe a WPA3-Personal-only WLAN? Choose two.
options: It uses SAE for password-based authentication
It requires TKIP for compatibility with original WPA
It requires protected management frame support
It requires individual RADIUS accounts for every client
It removes the need to protect endpoints and credentials
explanation: WPA3-Personal authenticates with SAE and requires protected management frames (PMF). It does not remove endpoint or credential risks.

whyWrong.1: TKIP is obsolete and not part of WPA3-Personal.
whyWrong.3: Per-user RADIUS accounts are an Enterprise design.
whyWrong.4: Wireless security does not replace endpoint and credential protection.

exhibit.title: netsh wlan show interfaces — representative
exhibit.text:
State: connected
SSID: STAFF
Authentication: WPA2-Personal
Cipher: CCMP
Channel: 44
Receive rate (Mbps): 866.7

prompt: What does this report show about the client's security?
options: The client is using an Enterprise EAP method against RADIUS
The client has completed a successful application throughput test
The connection uses TKIP because Personal mode requires RC4
The connection uses WPA2-Personal with the reported CCMP cipher
explanation: The Authentication field says Personal and the Cipher field says CCMP, so the connection uses WPA2-Personal with CCMP.

whyWrong.0: The report says Personal, not Enterprise.
whyWrong.1: A link rate is not a throughput test.
whyWrong.2: The reported cipher is CCMP, not TKIP.

prompt: Which two 802.11 standards operate only in the 5 GHz band? Choose two.
explanation: 802.11a and 802.11ac use only 5 GHz. 802.11b and g use 2.4 GHz, and 802.11n and ax use both bands.

whyWrong.1: 802.11b uses only 2.4 GHz.
whyWrong.2: 802.11g uses only 2.4 GHz.
whyWrong.3: 802.11n uses both 2.4 and 5 GHz.

prompt: Which encryption protocol did the original WPA introduce to replace WEP on existing hardware?
options: AES-CCMP
TKIP
GCMP-256
SAE
explanation: WPA introduced TKIP, which keeps the RC4 cipher but changes the key for each packet. WPA2 replaced it with AES-CCMP.

whyWrong.2: GCMP-256 belongs to WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode.
whyWrong.3: SAE is a WPA3-Personal authentication method, not an encryption protocol.

prompt: What does a BSSID identify?
options: The network name that a user selects to join the WLAN
The group of APs that advertise the same network name
One basic service set: an AP radio serving one SSID
The VLAN in which the AP places its wireless clients
explanation: A BSSID identifies one basic service set, in MAC-address format. An AP uses a different BSSID for each SSID on each radio.

whyWrong.0: The network name is the SSID.
whyWrong.1: APs sharing an SSID form an ESS, and each has its own BSSID.
whyWrong.3: A BSSID does not identify a VLAN.

exhibit.title: Windows-style scan — representative
exhibit.text:
SSID: STAFF
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:50   Band: 2.4 GHz   Channel: 6
BSSID: 02:11:22:33:44:51   Band: 5 GHz     Channel: 44

prompt: What can you conclude from this scan without an AP inventory?
options: Two BSSIDs advertise STAFF; the scan does not establish physical ownership
The different bands require the clients to use two different network names
The two identifiers establish that both radios belong to one physical AP
The similar addresses establish that the second entry is a spoofed radio
explanation: One SSID can be advertised by several radios, each with its own BSSID. Similar BSSIDs do not show which physical AP owns them.

whyWrong.1: Both bands can advertise the same SSID.
whyWrong.2: Similar addresses do not show the radios are in one AP.
whyWrong.3: A similar BSSID does not show spoofing.

prompt: An AP changes from 20 dBm transmit power to 23 dBm. What is its approximate new power?
options: 50 mW
400 mW
200 mW
explanation: 20 dBm is 100 mW, and each +3 dB doubles the power, so 23 dBm is about 200 mW.

whyWrong.0: About 50 mW is 17 dBm, a decrease.
whyWrong.1: About 400 mW is 26 dBm.
whyWrong.3: 1,000 mW is 30 dBm.

prompt: At one receiver, signal is −65 dBm and noise is −92 dBm. What is the SNR?
options: 27 dBm
−157 dBm
27 dB
−27 dB
explanation: SNR in dB is signal minus noise: −65 − (−92) = 27 dB. It is a ratio, so the unit is dB, not dBm.

whyWrong.0: The number is right but the unit is wrong; SNR is in dB.
whyWrong.1: Adding the two levels does not give SNR.
whyWrong.3: This reverses the subtraction.

exhibit.title: Survey worksheet
exhibit.text:
AP-A: channel 1
AP-B: channel 6
AP-C: channel 6
AP-B and AP-C: strong mutual reception; high shared airtime utilization

prompt: All APs use 20 MHz channels in the 1/6/11 plan, and no other channel-11 source exists. Which change fixes the shown channel reuse?
options: Move AP-C to channel 11 and verify the resulting RF behavior
Move AP-A to channel 6 so all APs can coordinate one channel
Move AP-B to channel 3 to separate it from AP-C numerically
Move AP-C to channel 8 to create a separate center frequency
explanation: AP-B and AP-C share channel 6. Moving AP-C to channel 11 gives each AP its own channel in the 1/6/11 plan.

whyWrong.1: Moving AP-A to channel 6 adds a third AP on the same channel.
whyWrong.2: Channel 3 overlaps channels 1 and 6.
whyWrong.3: Channel 8 overlaps channel 6.

exhibit.title: Verified deployment
exhibit.text:
AP1: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:01:10
AP2: SSID STAFF, BSSID 02:00:00:00:02:10
Both bridge to VLAN 20 through the wired LAN.
The roaming client's address remains 10.20.0.57/24.

prompt: The managed deployment uses the same SSID and security on both APs with a common distribution system. What describes the combined service?
options: An independent basic service set
A single basic service set
An extended service set
A wireless mesh backhaul
explanation: Several APs with the same SSID and security, joined by a common distribution system, form an extended service set (ESS).

whyWrong.0: An IBSS is an ad hoc network with no infrastructure APs.
whyWrong.1: Each BSSID is a separate BSS, so there are two.
whyWrong.3: The exhibit shows wired distribution, not a wireless mesh.

exhibit.title: Authorized diagnostic observations — authored worksheet
exhibit.text:
2.4 GHz client: strong received level, heavy retries while nearby microwave runs
Spectrum observation: non-Wi-Fi energy increases during operation
Controlled appliance off/on trials: impairment repeatedly disappears/returns
5 GHz comparison client: unaffected

prompt: What do the controlled observations show?
options: The noon timing proves a neighboring AP changes channel
A DFS event on 2.4 GHz causes the recorded loss
The operating appliance is a demonstrated interference source
The laptop's strong signal rules out RF interference
explanation: The drops line up with the appliance running, and a non-Wi-Fi energy measurement confirms it. That makes the appliance an interference source.

whyWrong.0: No neighboring AP channel change is shown.
whyWrong.1: DFS is a 5 GHz feature, not 2.4 GHz.
whyWrong.3: A strong signal can coexist with interference.

prompt: A WLAN design must support revoking one employee's individual credential. Which design directly meets that requirement?
options: Personal mode with one shared passphrase and MAC filtering
Personal mode with one periodically rotated staff passphrase
Personal mode with one shared passphrase and hidden SSID
Enterprise EAP with an individually managed account per employee
explanation: Enterprise EAP gives each employee an individual account, so one credential can be disabled alone. Personal mode shares one passphrase with everyone.

whyWrong.0: MAC filtering is not individual authentication, and MAC addresses can be copied.
whyWrong.1: Rotating a shared passphrase affects all users, not one employee.
whyWrong.2: Hiding the SSID adds no individual credentials.

prompt: A point-to-point link needs a narrow beam aimed at a second building. Which antenna pattern fits?
options: An omnidirectional antenna covering the room horizontally
A directional dish with an 8-degree specified beamwidth
A broad wall-panel pattern covering a 120-degree sector
An omnidirectional ceiling pattern covering nearby desks
explanation: A directional dish with a narrow beamwidth concentrates the signal toward one point. Omnidirectional and wide-sector antennas spread the signal.

whyWrong.0: An omnidirectional antenna covers the whole room, not a narrow beam.
whyWrong.2: A 120-degree sector is far wider than a point-to-point link needs.
whyWrong.3: A ceiling omnidirectional pattern covers nearby desks.

exhibit.title: Client status
exhibit.text:
Receive PHY rate: 600 Mb/s
Client count on shared channel: 24
Application file-transfer rate: not measured

prompt: Why does the reported PHY rate not establish a 600 Mb/s file-transfer rate?
options: Each associated client is reserved the displayed 600 Mb/s concurrently
The application rate is fixed at exactly half the displayed PHY rate
Changing the SSID isolates this client from the channel's other users
Overhead and shared airtime prevent that link rate from proving throughput
explanation: The PHY rate is the link's raw radio speed. Airtime is shared among clients, and protocol overhead and retries reduce it, so file transfers are slower.

whyWrong.0: Clients share the channel; the rate is not reserved per client.
whyWrong.1: There is no fixed ratio between PHY rate and application throughput.
whyWrong.2: Changing the SSID does not separate the client from other users of the channel.

exhibit.title: Two RF measurements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Comparable readings at each client during the stated interval:
Client A: signal −54 dBm, noise −66 dBm
Client B: signal −66 dBm, noise −96 dBm
Application throughput has not been measured.

prompt: What do the two measurements show?
options: A has stronger signal and therefore must deliver higher throughput
A has 12 dBm SNR, while B has a weaker 30 dBm signal
B has 30 dB SNR, compared with A's 12 dB; throughput still needs testing
B must use a higher-power AP because its noise floor is lower
explanation: A has SNR −54 − (−66) = 12 dB and B has −66 − (−96) = 30 dB. B has the better SNR despite a weaker signal, but throughput still needs testing.

whyWrong.0: A stronger signal does not give better throughput when the noise is higher.
whyWrong.1: SNR is in dB, and −66 dBm is B's signal level, not A's SNR.
whyWrong.3: A lower noise floor says nothing about the AP's transmit power.

exhibit.title: Bonded channel comparison (exercise)
exhibit.text:
AP-A: 5 GHz, 80 MHz width; occupied component channels 36, 40, 44 and 48.
AP-B: 5 GHz, 20 MHz width on channel 44.
The cells have strong mutual reception.

prompt: Which channel-width conclusion is correct?
options: Different primary channels prove the occupied spectrum is independent
The 80 MHz radio overlaps the narrower radio's channel spectrum
Renaming one SSID separates these transmissions in frequency
Both must have the same PHY rate because some spectrum overlaps
explanation: An 80 MHz channel includes the 20 MHz channel 44, so the two transmissions overlap in frequency. Different primary channel numbers do not make them separate.

whyWrong.0: The primary channel does not describe the whole bonded range.
whyWrong.2: The SSID name does not change frequency.
whyWrong.3: Overlap does not make the PHY rates equal.

exhibit.title: Measurement location and time (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Laptop receive level from AP-A: −60 dBm at 10:00.
AP-A noise floor: −95 dBm at 10:20 in a different location.
No laptop noise measurement is available.

prompt: Can these two readings give the laptop's SNR?
options: No: obtain comparable signal and noise readings at the same receiver
Yes: subtract the distant AP's noise reading to obtain 35 dB
Yes: the shared SSID makes noise identical throughout the WLAN
No: negative dBm levels cannot be used in a subtraction
explanation: SNR needs the signal and noise measured at the same receiver at the same time. A laptop's signal and an AP's noise come from different receivers.

whyWrong.1: Subtracting an AP's noise from the laptop's signal mixes two receivers.
whyWrong.2: A shared SSID does not make noise the same everywhere.
whyWrong.3: Negative dBm values can be subtracted; the problem is mixing receivers.

exhibit.title: Band compatibility requirements (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Approved new WLAN: 6 GHz, WPA3-Personal.
Client vendor specification and driver report: 2.4/5 GHz only.
The business requires this client to retain authorized access; its current hardware has no 6 GHz upgrade path.

prompt: The client has no 6 GHz radio. Which change lets it keep access?
options: Rename the 6 GHz SSID to match the client's saved 5 GHz profile
Offer the WLAN on a band the client supports, or replace the client
Select WPA2-only security on the 6 GHz radio for this client
Increase 6 GHz transmit power until the client's adapter detects it
explanation: A client without 6 GHz can only use 2.4 or 5 GHz. Offer the WLAN on a band it supports or replace the client.

whyWrong.0: Matching the SSID does not give the client a 6 GHz radio.
whyWrong.2: WPA2 is not allowed on 6 GHz, and a security change does not add a band.
whyWrong.3: More power does not change which bands the adapter supports.

prompt: Two neighboring APs use 20 MHz channels 36 and 40 in the 5 GHz band. Why do these channels not overlap, when 2.4 GHz channels 1 and 2 do?
options: 5 GHz channel numbers are spaced so that their centers are 20 MHz apart
5 GHz signals are absorbed by walls before they can reach another cell
DFS moves one of the two APs whenever both transmit at the same time
5 GHz radios are full duplex, so two cells cannot interfere on a channel
explanation: 5 GHz channels are numbered in steps of four, so adjacent 20 MHz channels have centers 20 MHz apart and do not overlap. 2.4 GHz centers are only 5 MHz apart.

whyWrong.1: Neighboring 5 GHz cells still hear each other; the channel spacing keeps them separate.
whyWrong.2: DFS reacts to radar, not to other APs.
whyWrong.3: Wi-Fi radios are half duplex in every band.

prompt: A laptop receives AP-A at −70 dBm and AP-B at −60 dBm. How do the two received power levels compare?
options: AP-A's signal is ten times as strong as AP-B's
AP-B's signal is twice as strong as AP-A's
AP-B's signal is ten times as strong as AP-A's
AP-B's signal is 10 mW stronger than AP-A's
explanation: −60 dBm is stronger than −70 dBm. A 10 dB difference is a factor of ten in power.

whyWrong.0: This reverses the comparison; −60 dBm is the stronger.
whyWrong.1: Twice the power is 3 dB, not 10 dB.
whyWrong.3: A dB difference is a ratio, not milliwatts.

exhibit.title: A direction-specific RF change (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Same stationary client before/after an approved AP power increase:
Client receives AP: −72 -> −61 dBm.
AP receives client: −81 -> −81 dBm; uplink retries remain high.
Security completes; client address/gateway are correct.
Downloads improve, uploads still fail the application acceptance test.

prompt: The client hears the AP well, but uplink retries are high. What should you do next?
options: Raise the AP power again because the client hears it well
Inspect client-to-AP coverage and placement using repeated two-direction tests
Replace the DHCP pool because association implies good radio delivery
Widen the channel before checking the weak client-to-AP path
explanation: More AP power improved only what the client receives. The AP still hears a weak client, so check client-to-AP coverage, placement and obstructions with repeated two-way tests.

whyWrong.0: AP power does not raise the client's transmit power.
whyWrong.2: Association and valid addressing do not point to a DHCP problem.
whyWrong.3: A wider channel does not fix a weak uplink.

exhibit.title: Roaming and retained addressing (exercise)
exhibit.text:
AP-A and AP-B advertise STAFF with the same approved security.
Client was on AP-A/VLAN 20 with 10.20.0.57/24, gateway 10.20.0.1.
After moving: BSSID maps to AP-B; security succeeds; signal is strong.
The old IP settings remain, but the gateway and application no longer respond.
AP-B's wired VLAN/mobility mapping has not been verified.

prompt: After roaming to AP-B, the client keeps its address but IP traffic fails. What should you check next?
options: Treat the shared SSID as proof that both BSSIDs lead to VLAN 20
Raise the client signal threshold because strong RSSI proves DHCP succeeded
Change the server's address because a changed BSSID proves a server fault
Check AP-B's forwarding/VLAN design and the client's valid subnet after the move
explanation: The client associated and secured the link, but AP-B may map the SSID to a different VLAN. Check AP-B's VLAN design and whether the client's address fits that subnet.

whyWrong.0: The same SSID does not mean the same VLAN.
whyWrong.1: Good signal does not show DHCP succeeded or the subnet is correct.
whyWrong.2: Nothing shows a server address change.

exhibit.title: Two plausible interference explanations (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Lunchtime calls deteriorate on 2.4 GHz; signal stays strong.
Scan shows nearby APs; retries increase, but utilization and spectrum were not recorded.
A microwave is nearby, and client load also rises at lunchtime.
Security and IP settings remain valid.

prompt: Which test best separates the possible RF causes?
options: Declare the nearby microwave responsible because loss happens at lunch
Replace the shared passphrase because channel scans cannot show passwords
Change every AP to the strongest scanned channel and compare afterward
Record band, retries/utilization and spectrum during controlled authorized comparisons
explanation: Record the band, retries, utilization and spectrum during controlled comparisons. Change one factor at a time to separate non-Wi-Fi interference from Wi-Fi load.

whyWrong.0: The timing alone does not prove the oven is the cause.
whyWrong.1: No security failure is shown, and a passphrase change does not test RF.
whyWrong.2: The strongest channel is not the least congested, and changing every AP removes control.

prompt: How much power is 0 dBm?
options: 1 mW
0 mW
10 mW
100 mW
explanation: 0 dBm is 1 mW. Every +10 dB multiplies the power by ten, and every +3 dB doubles it.

whyWrong.1: 0 dBm is a reference level, not zero power.
whyWrong.2: 10 mW is 10 dBm.
whyWrong.3: 100 mW is 20 dBm.

prompt: Which cipher does WEP use?
options: RC4
AES-CCMP
TKIP
SAE
explanation: WEP uses RC4. WPA uses TKIP and WPA2 uses AES-CCMP.

whyWrong.1: AES-CCMP is used by WPA2.
whyWrong.2: TKIP is used by WPA.
whyWrong.3: SAE is the WPA3-Personal authentication method, not a cipher.

prompt: How does Enterprise mode authenticate users?
options: 802.1X with a RADIUS server
One shared passphrase
A MAC address list
A hidden SSID
explanation: Enterprise mode uses 802.1X with RADIUS, giving each user individual credentials. Personal mode shares one passphrase.

whyWrong.1: A shared passphrase is Personal mode.
whyWrong.2: A MAC list is not an authentication method.
whyWrong.3: A hidden SSID adds no authentication.

prompt: Which type of interference occurs when nearby APs use the same channel and share airtime?
options: Co-channel interference
Adjacent-channel interference
Non-Wi-Fi interference
Multipath fading
explanation: APs on the same channel share airtime, which is co-channel interference. Adjacent-channel interference comes from overlapping channels.

whyWrong.1: Adjacent-channel interference comes from overlapping, not identical, channels.
whyWrong.2: Non-Wi-Fi interference comes from devices such as microwave ovens and Bluetooth.
whyWrong.3: Multipath fading comes from reflected signals, not shared channels.
